title: The Emperor's Riddle on True Mortality (ES)
summary: Akbar asks what separates an emperor from a beggar after death. Birbal takes the Emperor to an ancient graveyard to find the answer. [ES]
full_text:
During a quiet evening walk outside the city walls, Emperor Akbar and Birbal passed an ancient, crumbling graveyard where kings, warriors, merchants, and beggars had been buried over five centuries.

Akbar paused, looking at the overgrown mounds of dust, and asked in a somber tone: 'Birbal, look at these graves. In life, emperors sleep on golden thrones and beggars sleep in the mud. What is the difference between a king and a beggar after death?'

Birbal walked among the broken tombstones, picked up two ancient, weathered human skulls from an eroded grave pit, and brought them to the Emperor.

Birbal held one skull in his right hand, and the other in his left hand.

Both skulls were grey, hollow, and weathered by centuries of rain and wind.

Birbal said: 'Your Majesty, examine these two skulls carefully.

'One belonged to an ancient, mighty emperor who commanded armies of a hundred thousand soldiers and ruled three kingdoms!

'The other belonged to a penniless beggar who walked barefoot and begged for crusts of barley bread!

'Tell me, Sire: which of these skulls is the emperor, and which is the beggar?'

Akbar looked at both skulls. They were completely identical. There were no crowns, no rags, no gold, and no poverty written upon the hollow bone.

Akbar whispered in deep humility: 'It is impossible to tell, Birbal. They are completely equal in the dust.'

Birbal nodded with profound solemnity:

'Yes, Your Majesty. Death is the great leveler of humanity. The grave asks not how many diamonds you wore, nor how many palaces you built.

'The only thing that survives the dust is the righteousness of your deeds, the justice you delivered, and the kindness you sowed in the hearts of your people. An emperor's crown rots in the soil, but his virtue shines in the presence of the Divine forever.'

Akbar bowed his head in reverence, and returned to the palace with a renewed commitment to justice and humility.
